questions.question: How do you implement and traverse a singly linked list in Go?
questions.title: How do you implement and traverse a singly linked list in Go
questions.direct_answer: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node. The head pointer identifies the first node, and `nil` marks the end. Traversal starts at the head and follows `Next` one node at a time. Insertion or deletion rewires pointers; finding a position still requires walking from the head unless its node is already known.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node. The head pointer identifies the first node, and `nil` marks the end.

Traversal starts at the head and follows `Next` one node at a time. Insertion or deletion rewires pointers; finding a position still requires walking from the head unless its node is already known.

For example, for `10 -> 20 -> 30`, inserting `15` after the first node sets the new node's `Next` to `20`, then changes the first node's `Next` to the new node.

Go's standard library rarely needs a custom singly linked list for ordinary application collections. Choose it for a matching access pattern, not because insertion is described as O(1) without including the search cost.

A linked list is useful when code already holds node positions and performs frequent local insertions or removals. It can also model chains whose nodes need stable addresses.

a singly linked list in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

sections.content:
